finding: The live range of $40-$550 is too low at the bottom and about right at the top. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks; 0.33-1.0 hr in every class): economy 2015 Corolla about $150-$383 ($109.99 Delphi to $222.87 Toyota list); midsize 2016 Accord about $104-$566 ($63.93 Hitachi to $405.72 Honda list); truck 2023 Tahoe 5.3L about $95-$264 ($55.31 to $104.38 GM list); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $182-$658 ($141.94 Bosch to $497.76 BMW list). The bottom: the lowest totals, about $95-$104, pair an online-priced sensor with 20 minutes of labor, less than most shops charge for either; the lowest benchmark is $158 (Jerry). Nothing found supports $40 for a shop replacement: that is roughly the cost of a can of sensor cleaner or a minimum labor charge. A floor near $100-$150 is supportable. The top: $550 fits RepairPal's $274-$381 and most of what we built, and is a little low only where a dealer-list part is used on the Accord (about $566) or a European luxury car (about $658 for the 328i). Two low ends need a caveat. The Tahoe low is not an aftermarket part: no aftermarket sensor for the 2023 Tahoe was found, so it is the genuine GM sensor at the lowest online price seen ($55.31 against a $104.38 list). The Accord low is a Hitachi sensor whose fit rests on a cross-reference to the Honda part number (37980-RC0-M01); neither retailer page that loaded prints the model years. The Accord list price is also uncertain: three catalog pages show $405.72 and the part's own page at the same dealer catalog shows $345.55 (which would make the top about $506); the figure three pages agree on was used. How solid the labor times are: weak. Only the Tahoe has a manufacturer-stated time (GM 1.0 hr), and that operation also replaces the wiring connector, so it overstates the sensor alone. For the Corolla, Accord and 328i no manufacturer time was found; the range rests on a mechanic-written consumer guide's 'book time is usually between 20 and 35 minutes' and a general 'no more than an hour of work' statement, neither vehicle-specific. Seven of the eight hour figures are not for the example vehicle, so confidence is low. The job itself is simple on most cars (a connector and two screws on the Accord), which is consistent with the short times. Parts are the bigger variable: list prices found run from $104 (Tahoe) to $498 (328i). Nothing is null.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis (one guide says 0.5-1.0 hr), since a MAF code is frequently caused by a dirty or oiled sensor, an air leak after the sensor, a loose intake tube or a clogged air filter rather than a failed sensor. A shop may clean the sensor first, replace the air filter, repair the wiring connector (one GM bulletin bundles the connector with the sensor at 1.0 hr), and add shop supplies and tax. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis.
